verdict.qualified.desc: The research supports the claim, with conditions on who it applies to, how much, or what kind of study.
verdict.partly.desc: The research supports part of the original claim. The rest is overstated or has no evidence behind it.
verdict.corrected.desc: The research does not support the numbers or the conclusion in the original claim.
verdict.no-direct.desc: The research did not measure deaths from any cause, so it cannot show whether this helps you live longer. That is not the same as showing that it does not work.
direction.helps.desc: The research found it goes with lower risk.
direction.harms.desc: The research found it goes with higher risk.
direction.no-effect.desc: The research found no clear change in risk either way. That does not prove it is useless for everyone.
direction.mixed.desc: The result changes with the amount, the group or the comparison, or its direction is not yet clear.
strength.label: Evidence strength
strength.A.desc: Randomized trials that compared deaths directly.
strength.B.desc: Large long-term studies, many studies pooled together, or randomized trials with some flaws.
strength.C.desc: Few people or few studies, or clear flaws in how the study was done.
strength.D.desc: Only indirect clues, such as animal studies or other health measures.
kind.observational: Observational, shows a link, not a cause
kind.trial.desc: Researchers split people into two groups by chance and compared them. Chance makes the groups alike in other ways, so the difference comes from the thing itself.
kind.observational.desc: Researchers followed a group of people over time and compared those who did the thing with those who did not. The groups may differ in other ways too, so this cannot prove the thing caused the difference.
kind.indirect.desc: It does not compare how long people in a study lived. It comes from animal studies, country-level statistics, reviews, drug labels or models, so treat it as a clue.

home.title: Want to live longer? See what the research says
home.lead: There are so many health claims that it is hard to tell which are true. This site explains {count} studies in plain words: what works, what does not, and how solid the evidence is.
home.figure.helps: {count} things worth doing, with strong evidence
home.figure.nohelp: {count} things that do not help, or do harm
home.figure.myths: {count} popular claims that do not hold up
home.helps.title: Worth doing
home.helps.intro: The {count} things where the evidence is strong and the research found a benefit. Trials in people already diagnosed with a disease are under "{illness}" instead.
home.nohelp.title: No help, or harmful
home.nohelp.intro: The {count} things where the evidence is strong but the research found no benefit, or found harm. Strong evidence means the answer is reliable, not that the thing is worth doing.
home.topics.title: Browse by topic
home.myths.title: Popular claims: true or false?
home.myths.intro: Of the popular claims checked here, {corrected} were wrong, {partly} were only partly right and {nodirect} had no direct evidence.
home.read.title: How to read these studies
home.read.strength.title: More bars, more reliable
home.read.grades: Every study has a four-bar evidence meter. It says how far you can trust the answer, not whether the thing is good for you.
home.read.observe.title: A link is not proof
home.read.association: Most studies follow a group of people for years and find that a habit goes with a longer life. But those people may also be younger, richer or less likely to smoke, so the study shows a link, not a cause. A randomized trial splits people into two groups by chance and compares them, which can show that the thing itself made the difference.
home.read.add.title: Numbers do not add up
home.read.additive: Each percentage compares two groups within one study. You cannot add up numbers from different studies, or turn them into years of life you would gain.
home.read.source: The research checks come from the open-source project {upstream}, and every verdict comes from it unchanged. This site writes the plain-language questions, answers and explanations from its data. They may simplify, and every page keeps the project's original text.
home.read.more: More on the method, the grades and the sources

about.title: About this site
about.lead: This site turns the research checks of HowToLiveLonger into pages you can read by topic. The medical content and the verdict on each claim come unchanged from that project. This site writes the plain-language question, answer and explanation on each page from the project's data, and they may simplify it. Every page keeps the project's full text under "Want the raw data?".
about.method.title: Where the content comes from
about.method.text: HowToLiveLonger began as "A Programmer's Guide to Longevity", a list of longevity claims and numbers. Its reviewers later looked up each cited paper. For every claim they recorded the effect estimate, the interval, the comparison and the study population, judged whether the claim holds, and noted which part of the paper they read. {original} records come from the original guide and {added} were added during the review.
about.method.limits: This is not a systematic review. For most sources the reviewers read only the abstract. On each study page, "What was read in each paper" under "Want the raw data?" says what was read. The letter grades are the project's own practical scale, not a formal GRADE assessment.
about.grades.title: Evidence grades
about.directions.title: Helps or harms
about.directions.intro: This site adds the label, based on the effect estimate, interval, comparison and findings recorded upstream. An interval that crosses 1, or a finding of no significant difference, counts as no effect found. A direction that is unclear, or that changes with the amount or the group, counts as mixed or unclear. The upstream text is unchanged.
about.kinds.title: Kinds of evidence
about.kinds.intro: This site also adds this label. It sorts each study by its design, which decides whether the evidence can show cause and effect.
about.verdicts.title: Four verdicts on the original claims
about.disclaimer.title: Not medical advice
about.disclaimer.text: This site summarizes published research to help you judge health claims. It cannot replace a clinician's judgement about your own situation. If you have symptoms, take medication or plan to change a treatment, talk to a clinician first.
about.source.title: Source and license
about.source.text: The content comes from {repo} at commit {commit} ({date}), released into the public domain under the Unlicense. The cited papers have their own terms.
about.source.kit: The interface uses the 小小东 UI Kit under the PolyForm Noncommercial license.
about.contribute.title: How to contribute
about.contribute.text: If a number, population or conclusion is wrong, propose a change to HowToLiveLonger following {guide}. Include the original paper, the study design, the population, the comparison and the interval. After the change lands upstream, this site picks it up on the next sync.
about.contribute.site: For problems with this site's layout, interface text or translations, open an issue in {repo}.
